# The Weight of Ordinary Things

I've been thinking about how we carry invisible loads every day. Not the backpacks or grocery bags—those are simple, measurable. I mean the other things. The way a song can suddenly make you remember someone you haven't thought about in years. The small obligation you forgot about three weeks ago that still nags at you. The text message you received that you haven't answered because you don't know what to say.

This morning I watched a man at the coffee shop stare into his cup for what must have been five minutes. Not drinking. Just staring. I wondered what he was carrying. Does he have a deadline? A conversation he needs to have? Is someone mad at him? Is he mad at himself? We pass hundreds of people every day, and almost none of them look light.

I think we've normalized heaviness to such an extent that we barely notice it anymore. We collect small weights the way you might collect lint in a pocket—gradually, without intention, until one day you reach in and realize how much has accumulated. A promise you made. A skill you meant to learn. A person you meant to call. These things stack up in the dark spaces of our minds, and we develop an entire posture around them. We hunch. We look down. We move through the world as though we're always descending a slight incline.

The remarkable thing is that nobody assigns these weights to us. We volunteer for them. Or sometimes they're placed on us so gradually that we can't remember when we first picked them up. A parent might mention, casually over dinner years ago, that they worried about you. Now you're an adult and you're still trying to solve that worry. A teacher might have suggested you weren't artistic. Now you don't even try. A childhood friend moved away. You don't reach out because it's been too long. That silence becomes a weight—the silence itself, the gap that grows wider with time.

I wonder if birds feel this way, or if they're just light. They shake themselves off and move on. I've never seen a pigeon look burdened by its past. Maybe that's wisdom. Maybe that's just neurology.

What strikes me is how we think about lightness wrong. We imagine it as the absence of things—an empty room, a blank schedule, a person with no obligations. But I think actual lightness might be something else entirely. It might be about knowing what things matter and being willing to let everything else fall away. It might be about clarity instead of emptiness.

There's a woman I know who seems genuinely light. Not because her life is simple—it isn't. She has problems like everyone else. But something about the way she moves through the world is different. She says no to things without guilt. She talks about her failures like someone discussing the weather. When she forgets something, she doesn't punish herself. She just remembers it or she doesn't. I've been trying to understand this quality, to reverse-engineer it, but I'm not sure it works that way. It's not a technique you can learn from a book. It's more like a permission you give yourself, and I'm not even sure how you get that permission.

Maybe it comes from being hurt enough that you realize you're still standing. Maybe it comes from loving someone so much that you understand they're going to disappoint you and it's okay. Maybe it comes from failing publicly and learning that the sky doesn't fall.

I've been carrying something for months. It's not enormous—it's the kind of weight that most people wouldn't notice on you. It's the weight of uncertainty about something I need to decide. And I notice how this weight changes depending on my posture toward it. Some days I hold it in front of me and stare at it and it seems enormous—full of implications and dangers. Other days I just let it sit on my shoulders and go about my business, and it becomes almost invisible. The weight hasn't changed. My attention has.

Maybe that's the secret. Not removing the weights, but changing our relationship to them.

There's something honorable about carrying things, actually. It means you care about something. It means you're taking responsibility. A person with no weight at all might just be someone who doesn't care about anything. That's not lightness—that's emptiness. The goal isn't to care about nothing. The goal is to care about the right things and trust that you can carry them without bending.

I'm not sure I believe that yet, but I'm working on it.

The man at the coffee shop eventually picked up his cup and drank the coffee, which was probably cold by then. He made a small face like it tasted bad, and then he left. I don't know if he felt any lighter when he walked out. But he did walk out. He got up and he moved forward. Maybe that's all any of us can do—not wait until we're light enough to move, but move anyway, carrying everything we're carrying, trusting that the act of moving will eventually change something.

I think if I had one piece of advice for people, it would be this: notice what you're carrying. Don't let it be invisible. Bring it into the light and look at it. Ask yourself if you chose it or if it was placed on you. Ask yourself if you still want it. Some things we can put down. Some things we'll keep carrying forever, and that's okay—they're important to us. But at least we can know what they are. At least we can walk with intention instead of just finding ourselves slowly bent over, unable to remember when we became this way.

The lightness we're seeking might not be the absence of weight. It might just be clarity about what we're carrying and why.
